tasks.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention › Diagnostic systems, 3rd paragraph; Management › Cannabis withdrawal, 1st-2nd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC8655458 (NIH author manuscript of Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7:16), as read by the first reader
tasks.extracted: DSM-5 withdrawal in the Primer's words: three or more signs within 1 week of cessation (irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; decreased appetite or weight loss; restlessness; depressed mood; at least one physical symptom causing severe discomfort, such as abdominal pain, shakiness, sweating, fever, chills or headache), which must cause clinically severe distress or impairment (the Primer's wording; reduced use is not mentioned). Many of these symptoms also occur in other substance withdrawal or in other mental disorders. Second-hand: symptoms typically begin 24-48 hours after stopping, peak within the first week and last 1-2 weeks (Budney et al., 2003); 12% of people who use frequently had DSM-5 withdrawal in the past 12 months in a US national sample (Livne et al., 2019). In Management, Bahji et al.'s figures are relabelled as 12-17% in the general population of people who use cannabis and as 54% of outpatients and 87% of inpatients with a use disorder seeking treatment reporting clinically severe withdrawal. Without medical or psychiatric comorbidity, withdrawal is said not to pose serious risks, with most people needing only supportive care, in a sentence that cites no source.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Strengths and limitations of this study (box), 3rd to 5th bullets
tasks.extracted: The authors state that women who use cannabis often also smoke tobacco or drink alcohol and that most included studies did not exclude polysubstance use, so a cannabis-only effect could not be determined: it is unknown whether the associations relate to cannabis or to tobacco and alcohol use, tobacco and heavy alcohol use being, the authors say, established causes of low birth weight, preterm birth and small-for-gestational-age births. Few outcomes were measured or defined in a standard way, and reliance on self-report may have led to under-reporting of use.
